extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, designers, and preservationists
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and aesthetic standards for designing domestic and public architecture that endures, records history, and balances essential form with picturesque effects. Emphasizes duties to posterity, material-appropriate style choice, meaningful ornament, and building as memorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render the architecture of the day historical
rubrics_metrics.description: “the first, to render the architecture of the day, historical” — architecture of the present should be made memorial or monumental so that true perfection is attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design new buildings so they can be read as records of their time: aim for monumentality and for decorations animated by metaphorical or historical meaning. Build with stability and with elements that communicate civic or social significance to future ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the architecture of past ages as the most precious inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: “the second, to preserve, as the most precious of inheritances, that of past ages.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat historical fabric as an invaluable bequest; maintenance and conservation are moral duties on par with creating new work. Respect continuity between past and present in planning and intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic buildings should be built to last beyond one generation
rubrics_metrics.description: “a people when their houses are built to last for one generation only” is an evil sign; houses should not be swept away soon as room is made for new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design dwellings for durability and continuance: avoid ephemeral tenements and temporary construction. Prioritize foundations, materials, and workmanship that allow homes to become lasting family monuments and sources of inherited affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the house as a temple and record of a life
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is a sanctity in a good man's house... I look upon those pitiful concretions... as temples — temples which we should hardly dare to injure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit the house to express moral worth and personal history. Respect the first builder's rights and the house's role as memorial; consider leaving inscribed stones or spaces to record the builder's life so the dwelling functions as a domestic monument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build houses to express each person's character, occupation, and history
rubrics_metrics.description: houses should be "built... with such differences as might suit and express each man's character and occupation, and partly his history."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt scale, ornament, and plan to reflect the inhabitant's identity and the building’s social role; avoid uniform, anonymous rows that erase personal and local distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public buildings must have a definite historical or symbolic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: “In public buildings the historical purpose should be still more definite.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sculpture, bas-relief, and ornament to record national feeling, achievement, or story. Decorations on civic buildings should communicate meaning—ideally symbolically when literal depiction is impractical—and contribute to the building’s civic narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply ornament without intellectual intention
rubrics_metrics.description: “There should not be a single ornament put upon great civic building-s, without some intellectual intention.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every ornament should be justified by thought: prefer the simplest element that conveys a story or fact to rich ornamentation that lacks meaning. Use variety where it serves narrative or symbolic purpose; avoid decorative emptiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer rudest work that tells a story to the richest without meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: “Better the rudest work that tells a story or records a fact, than the richest without meaning.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize communicative clarity and historical record over luxurious but empty decoration. Even modest execution is superior if it serves narrative or moral ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build with regard to posterity — practice self-denial for future generations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The idea of self-denial for the sake of posterity... of planting forests that our descendants may live under their shade... these are our duties.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan and execute works with long-term benefits in mind: economic restraint today can be an ethical investment for successors. Consider ecological and urban legacies as part of architectural duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build for age — the greatest glory of a building is in its age
rubrics_metrics.description: “The greatest glory of a building is not in its stones, or in its gold. Its glory is in its Age... It is in that golden stain of time, that we are to look for the real light... of architecture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design so that the building will gain dignity and meaning over centuries. Choose details and compositions with an eye to their appearance after long weathering; value the 'voicefulness' and witness that age gives structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize arrangement of larger masses over perishable details
rubrics_metrics.description: “the arrangement of the larger masses being always a matter of greater importance than the treatment of the smaller”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the building’s primary composition, massing, and structural clarity are enduring; details should not be essential to the building’s impressiveness if they are likely to perish. Sacrifice transient ornament rather than lasting qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid depending for impressiveness upon perishable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: “taking care that for work of this kind we sacrifice no enduring quality, and that the building shall not depend for its impressiveness upon anything that is perishable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When incorporating delicate or temporary ornament, ensure it does not undermine the building’s long-term legibility and dignity. Favor materials and details whose weathering contributes positively or at least does not destroy essential form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and control the picturesque (Parasitical Sublimity)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Picturesqueness... is Parasitical Sublimity... the second [essential to picturesque] the subordinate or parasitical position of that sublimity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when picturesque effects (accidental lights, shadows, excrescential ornament) are appropriate and when they degrade essential character. Picturesqueness arises when sublimity depends on accidental or surface qualities; use it knowingly rather than by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let accidental or extraneous beauty override inherent character
rubrics_metrics.description: “the artist who looks to the stem of the ivy instead of the shaft of the pillar, is carrying out... the debased sculptor's choice of the hair instead of the countenance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the building's inherent architectural identity rather than privileging surface effects (ivy, stains, exotic surface ornament) that obscure original character. If extraneous sublimity is adopted, integrate it so it remains consistent with the architecture's essential form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose architectural style according to material durability
rubrics_metrics.description: “styles of architecture which are picturesque... do not suffer, but commonly gain in richness of effect when their details are partly worn away; hence such styles... should always be adopted when the materials to be employed are liable to degradation... styles... dependent on purity of line... must be practised altogether in hard and undecomposing materials.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match style to available materials: use 'picturesque' (shade-dependent) styles for soft, weathering materials (brick, sandstone, soft limestone); reserve line-pure styles (Italian Gothic/classical) for hard, durable stones (granite, crystalline marbles). Let the expected weathering inform stylistic choice and detailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: When representing history in sculpture, use bold symbols to overcome costume difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: “Actual representation of history has... been checked by a difficulty... of unmanageable costume; nevertheless, by a sufficiently bold imaginative treatment, and frank use of symbols, all such obstacles may be vanquished.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When literal historical depiction is impractical, employ symbolic, imaginative devices in sculpture and bas-relief so the intended historical meaning remains legible and expressive within decorative constraints.
